I woke up at like 4am and couldn't go back to bed, and didn't feel like working, so I had a conversation with Cursor to get a better idea of what tools it has access to, and how they work.
Notebooks are great for giving clear instructions and adding/removing them as context at-will
Cursor grabs file context in 250-line chunks, so I now avoid having any files > 250 lines (and have it create a new file for anything that exceeds 250)
keep related code in single files when possible
I also coaxed Cursor into telling me exactly what tools it (allegedly) has access to. I think understanding its capabilities is a good starting point for how you're handling your codebase:
- Semantic code search (codebase_search) to find relevant code snippets based on meaning
- Text-based pattern search (grep_search) for finding exact matches or regex patterns
- File path search (file_search) to locate files with fuzzy matching
- Directory listing (list_dir) to explore the codebase structure
- Read file contents (read_file) to analyze code, with ability to read specific line ranges
- Edit existing files (edit_file) to modify code with precise changes
- Reapply edits (reapply) if an edit needs to be attempted again with a smarter model
- Run terminal commands (run_terminal_cmd) with your approval
- Execute commands in background when needed
- Handle git operations and other CLI tasks
- Plan and execute parallel edits (parallel_apply) across multiple files
- Apply similar changes to multiple locations efficiently
- Handle up to 50 files in a single batch operation
Each of these tools has specific parameters and best practices that I follow to ensure safe and effective code modifications.

For anyone like me who's interested in the internals of Cursor:
For files that are manually attached to context (but are not @-referenced), Cursor (claims it) uses the filename to determine whether or not it should actually read the file.
So, based on your request, it may not bother reading what's in context if it thinks it has what it needs already!
For this reason, I've added "ALWAYS READ" to the start of my Agent Rules file that I keep in permanent context, to increase its chances of being considered in any given scenario.
